description: The receptor tyrosine kinase MET, activated by hepatocyte growth factor, controls epithelial cell scattering, wound closure and invasive growth, and its coupling to tensin proteins at focal adhesions links that signal to how a cell grips and pulls on its substrate. At adhesion sites MET associates with tensin family members whose expression tends to be reciprocal: TNS4 stabilises the receptor and favours motility, while TNS3 predominates in less migratory states. Because tensins bridge the cytoplasmic tail of beta-1 integrin to the actin cytoskeleton, this interaction places growth factor signalling directly onto the adhesion machinery that determines migration speed and direction. Elevated TNS4 accompanies MET-driven invasion in carcinomas, making this branch of MET signalling relevant to metastatic behaviour rather than to proliferation alone.

Neuropilins are short-tailed cell-surface receptors that bind selected VEGF family ligands and hand them to the signalling VEGF receptors, so this set describes how ligand presentation tunes endothelial responsiveness during blood and lymphatic vessel growth. NRP1 captures the heparin-binding isoform VEGF-A165 along with VEGF-B and PlGF-2, while NRP2 additionally binds VEGF-A145 and VEGF-C, and both associate laterally with KDR (VEGFR-2) or FLT1 (VEGFR-1) to raise their affinity for particular ligands rather than to signal by their own kinase activity, since they have none. The consequence is isoform-selective control of endothelial proliferation, migration and sprouting, with NRP1 weighted toward arterial and angiogenic vessels and NRP2 toward veins and lymphatics. Loss of neuropilin function disrupts vascular patterning in development, and the same co-receptor interface is exploited in tumour angiogenesis and targeted by anti-angiogenic strategies.

Growth factor binding to the EGF receptor does more than switch on kinase cascades; one branch of its output runs through phospholipid turnover, and that is what this pathway captures. Any of several ligands — EGF, TGF-alpha, amphiregulin, epiregulin, epigen, betacellulin or heparin-binding EGF — dimerises and autophosphorylates the receptor, creating docking sites that recruit phospholipase C-gamma1 through its SH2 domains. Once tyrosine phosphorylated at the membrane, PLCG1 cleaves phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate into inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol, so a single receptor event raises cytosolic calcium released from internal stores and activates protein kinase C. The resulting calcium and PKC signals feed into proliferation, migration and cytoskeletal remodelling in epithelia, and inappropriate output from this arm contributes to the growth and invasiveness of EGFR-driven carcinomas.

Endothelial cells divide in response to VEGF, and this is the branch of VEGFR2 signalling that drives that proliferation — the basis of angiogenesis in development, wound healing and tumour vascularisation, and the target of anti-VEGF drugs. VEGFA binding to the KDR receptor triggers Src-dependent phosphorylation of the receptor tail, which recruits and activates phospholipase C gamma; the resulting inositol trisphosphate opens IP3 receptor channels on the endoplasmic reticulum, releasing calcium that, with calmodulin, cooperates with diacylglycerol to activate conventional protein kinase C isoforms. PKC then feeds into the Ras/Raf/MEK/ERK cascade, either by phosphorylating Raf directly or by acting on Ras itself — here through relief of GTPase-activating protein restraint rather than exchange-factor recruitment. Sphingosine kinase and PDPK1 add further lipid and kinase input, linking the same receptor to survival as well as growth.

Hepatocyte growth factor binding to the receptor tyrosine kinase MET triggers a survival and growth response, and one major branch of it runs through PI3K to AKT. This arm supports epithelial cell survival, motility and tissue regeneration in liver, kidney and skin, and is a principal reason MET-driven tumours resist apoptosis and invade. Activated MET autophosphorylates and recruits GRB2, which brings the multi-site adaptor GAB1 to the receptor; MET then phosphorylates GAB1 to create docking sites for the PI3K regulatory subunit PIK3R1. The associated PIK3CA catalytic subunit converts PIP2 to PIP3 at the membrane, recruiting AKT for activation and thereby suppressing pro-apoptotic effectors and promoting mTOR-dependent growth. MET amplification or activating mutation, or excess HGF in the stroma, keeps this signal on and is targeted by MET kinase inhibitors.

The receptor tyrosine kinase ERBB4 can act directly in the nucleus as well as at the cell surface, and nuclear signaling by ERBB4 is how neuregulin ligands are converted into changes in gene expression rather than kinase cascades alone. Neuregulin or EGF-family binding to juxtamembrane-A isoforms triggers ectodomain shedding by ADAM17, followed by gamma-secretase cleavage (presenilins with nicastrin, APH1 and PSENEN) that liberates a soluble intracellular domain into the cytosol. This fragment shuttles transcription factors into the nucleus and serves as their co-factor: with TAB2 and the corepressor NCOR1 it suppresses astrocytic genes such as GFAP and S100B in neural precursors, with STAT5A it drives beta-casein transcription during lactation, and with estrogen receptor it promotes progesterone receptor and CXCL12 expression. Competing WW-domain partners YAP1 and the tumour suppressor WWOX set whether the fragment reaches the nucleus, linking this axis to mammary differentiation and breast cancer.

Signalling through the ERBB4 receptor tyrosine kinase, one of the EGF receptor family, is terminated by ubiquitin-dependent destruction of the receptor and its cleavage fragments, and this downregulation sets how much growth-factor input from neuregulins a cell converts into proliferation, differentiation or nuclear gene regulation. Excessive or unopposed ERBB4 signalling contributes to tumour growth, while the same restraint shapes heart and nervous system development where ERBB4 acts. WW-domain motifs in the receptor's cytoplasmic tail recruit the NEDD4-family E3 ligases WWP1, ITCH and NEDD4, which attach ubiquitin to intact ERBB4 and to its membrane-anchored and soluble intracellular cleavage products, routing them to proteasomal and lysosomal degradation. Ubiquitination of the soluble fragment limits the pool that can enter the nucleus to act as a transcriptional co-regulator. Binding by these ligases does not require receptor activation, and SRC-mediated phosphorylation modulates the outcome.

This is the step that converts a ligand-bound, autophosphorylated EGF receptor into active RAS, and it is the canonical textbook route from a growth factor at the cell surface to proliferation. Any of several ligands — EGF, TGF-alpha, amphiregulin, epiregulin, epigen, betacellulin or heparin-binding EGF — dimerises the receptor and triggers phosphorylation of its cytoplasmic tail. The adaptor GRB2 docks on those phosphotyrosines through its SH2 domain while holding the guanine nucleotide exchange factor SOS1 through its SH3 domains, so receptor binding delivers SOS1 to the plasma membrane next to HRAS, KRAS and NRAS, where it promotes GDP-to-GTP exchange. Output feeds the MAP kinase cascade and downstream transcriptional programmes for growth and survival. Because the link is so direct, activating EGFR or RAS mutations drive lung, colorectal and other carcinomas, and determine whether receptor-blocking therapy can work.

Growth factor receptors of the ERBB family do more than drive proliferation: when ERBB2 partners with EGFR, ERBB3 or ERBB4 after ligand binding, it also steers where a cell goes. This motility arm matters for epithelial wound closure and morphogenesis, and its hyperactivation in ERBB2-amplified breast cancer contributes to invasion and metastasis rather than growth alone. Ligands such as EGF, betacellulin, heregulins and HB-EGF trigger receptor dimerisation and phosphorylation, creating a docking site for MEMO1. MEMO1 in turn holds active RHOA and its effector DIAPH1, a formin, at the plasma membrane, so that actin polymerisation and microtubule capture are coordinated at the leading edge. The result is directed lamellipodial protrusion and stabilised cell polarity, linking receptor tyrosine kinase signalling to cytoskeletal remodelling and migration.

Blood and lymphatic vessels grow where endothelial cells receive a vascular endothelial growth factor signal, and that signal begins with ligand binding to a VEGF receptor and the receptor pairing up. The step initiates cascades that drive endothelial proliferation, survival, migration and increased vascular permeability, and it is the point at which tumours recruit their own blood supply and the target of anti-angiogenic drugs. Secreted ligands including VEGFA, VEGFB, placental growth factor and the lymphangiogenic VEGFC and VEGFD engage the receptor tyrosine kinases FLT1, KDR and FLT4 with distinct preferences; receptors mainly form homodimers, though FLT1-KDR heterodimers occur. KDR carries most angiogenic signalling in vivo, FLT1 acts largely as a modulating or decoy receptor, and FLT4 specifies lymphatic endothelium. Loss or dysregulation underlies vascular malformations, lymphoedema and pathological neovascularisation in retinopathy and cancer.

ERBB4 is a receptor tyrosine kinase for neuregulins and several EGF-family ligands, and one branch of its output is the recruitment of phosphoinositide 3-kinase to the activated receptor. This arm supports cell survival, migration and differentiation in the nervous system, heart and mammary epithelium, where neuregulin-ERBB4 signalling guides neuronal migration, synapse formation, cardiomyocyte maturation and lactational differentiation; disrupted signalling has been linked to cardiomyopathy and to schizophrenia risk. Ligands such as NRG1-NRG4, betacellulin, epiregulin and HB-EGF drive receptor dimerisation and trans-autophosphorylation. Only the CYT1 splice isoforms retain the C-terminal tyrosine that docks the PI3K regulatory subunit p85 alpha; the p110 alpha catalytic subunit is then brought in, and the assembled kinase converts PIP2 to PIP3 to activate AKT. CYT2 isoforms lack this site, so alternative splicing determines whether a cell couples ERBB4 to survival signalling at all.

Turning on the MET receptor tyrosine kinase is a two-step affair, and this pathway covers both: the proteolytic maturation of hepatocyte growth factor and the ligand-driven dimerization of MET itself. The output is a signal that drives epithelial cell survival, scattering, motility and branching morphogenesis, and that underpins liver and placental development as well as wound repair and tissue regeneration. HGF is secreted as an inert single-chain precursor and must be cleaved by a membrane-anchored serine protease such as hepsin or by the extracellular activator HGFAC; the Kunitz-domain inhibitors SPINT1 and SPINT2 restrain those proteases and so set how much active ligand is available. Mature HGF engages the SEMA and PSI domains of MET, promoting receptor pairing and trans-autophosphorylation that both raises kinase activity and creates docking sites for adaptors. Excessive MET activation is a recurrent driver of invasive carcinoma.

Hepatocyte growth factor binding to the MET receptor makes cells move, and the route from receptor to movement runs through focal adhesion kinase. MET activates PTK2 signaling only when PTK2 is engaged simultaneously by MET and by integrins contacting the extracellular matrix, so the pathway couples a soluble growth factor cue to the adhesive state of the cell; SRC phosphorylation is required for PTK2 to reach full activity. The matrix side is supplied by fibronectin, fibrillar and fibril-associated collagens and the laminin chains that build basement membranes, read out through collagen- and laminin-binding integrins that pair alpha subunits with beta1. The output is adhesion turnover and directed migration, as in wound epithelialisation and branching morphogenesis, and the same axis drives invasion and metastasis when MET is amplified or HGF is supplied by tumour stroma.

After hepatocyte growth factor binds MET, the activated receptor is internalised rather than simply switched off, and its route through the endosomal system determines how long and how strongly it signals. Recycling of MET back to the plasma membrane sustains ERK1/ERK2 and STAT3 output, supporting the motility, scattering and invasive growth responses that HGF elicits in epithelial cells and that are hijacked in carcinoma progression. Endocytosed receptor is sorted by the adaptor GGA3 through RAB4A/RAB4B-marked early recycling endosomes and returned to the surface with help from ARF6, while adaptors GRB2, GAB1 and the CRK/CRKL pair remain bound and continue to relay signals from the endosome itself. Diverting MET toward degradation instead of recycling shortens the response, so this trafficking step acts as a control point on receptor tyrosine kinase signal duration.

Hepatocyte growth factor binding to the MET receptor tyrosine kinase triggers one branch of downstream signalling in which STAT3 is recruited and activated, linking a growth factor cue at the cell surface to changes in transcription that drive scattering, morphogenesis and invasive growth. STAT3 docks at a phosphorylated tyrosine in the MET carboxy-terminal tail, directly or via a scaffold, and is itself phosphorylated on Y705, which allows dimerization, nuclear entry and target gene expression; SRC activity contributes to this phosphorylation, and continued signalling from endosomes after MET internalization sustains it. The output is anchorage-independent proliferation and increased motility, which is why this axis is scrutinized in carcinomas where MET is amplified or HGF is produced in an autocrine loop. In normal physiology the same route supports epithelial repair, liver regeneration and branching morphogenesis.

Growth signalling through the ERBB2:ERBB3 heterodimer has to be switched off as well as switched on, and this negative feedback arm sets how much ERBB3 remains available at the cell surface. Neuregulin binding to ERBB3 and pairing with ERBB2 activates AKT; the same AKT activity phosphorylates and stabilises the deubiquitinase USP8, which reverses self-ubiquitination of the E3 ligase RNF41. Stabilised RNF41 then ubiquitinates ERBB3 and sends it for degradation, so receptor output limits its own duration. When RNF41 levels are low, ERBB3 persists on the membrane and sensitivity to neuregulin rises. Loss of this brake contributes to sustained PI3K/AKT signalling in breast and other epithelial cancers, where ERBB3 retention is one route to resistance against ERBB2-directed therapy, making receptor turnover part of the control of proliferation and survival.

Growth factor receptors must be switched off as reliably as they are switched on, and this pathway describes how ligand-activated EGFR is removed from the cell surface and destroyed so that signalling is limited in strength and duration. Loss of this braking system leaves the receptor chronically active, a route to transformation exploited by many epithelial tumours. After EGF, TGFA, amphiregulin or another ligand triggers autophosphorylation, the RING ubiquitin ligase CBL is recruited directly and through GRB2 and attaches ubiquitin to the receptor. The adaptor SH3KBP1 (CIN85) links CBL to endophilins, which bend membranes during clathrin-coated pit formation, while EPS15 and epsin read the ubiquitin mark and HGS/STAM sort the cargo into multivesicular bodies for lysosomal degradation rather than recycling. Phosphatases such as PTPN12 and Sprouty proteins add further negative feedback on receptor and downstream kinase output.

Growth factor receptors of the ERBB family can steer cells toward motility and calcium-dependent responses rather than simply proliferation, and the PLCG1 arm of ERBB2 signalling is how that branch is engaged. Ligand-bound EGFR pairs with ERBB2 as a heterodimer, and phospholipase C gamma 1 docks on specific phosphotyrosines in the receptor C-terminal tails, notably Y992 and Y1173 of EGFR. Once recruited and activated, PLCG1 hydrolyses phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate to inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol, releasing calcium from intracellular stores and activating protein kinase C. The output feeds into actin remodelling, cell migration and secretion, and contributes to the invasive behaviour of ERBB2-amplified breast tumours. Because this route depends on heterodimer formation rather than ERBB2 alone, it illustrates how receptor partner choice determines which second messengers a growth signal produces.

Hepatocyte growth factor binding to the MET receptor tyrosine kinase reshapes the cytoskeleton and makes epithelial cells move, and this branch of MET signalling is how that happens: activation of the small GTPases RAP1 and RAC1. The output is cell scattering, lamellipodium formation, spreading and integrin-dependent adhesion, processes used in wound healing, liver regeneration and embryonic morphogenesis, and hijacked by carcinomas for invasion and metastasis. Mechanistically, the activated receptor recruits GRB2 and the scaffolding adaptor GAB1, whose phosphorylated tyrosines bind the SH2/SH3 adaptors CRK and CRKL. These adaptors in turn dock guanine nucleotide exchange factors at the membrane: RAPGEF1 loads GTP onto RAP1A and RAP1B to strengthen adhesion, while DOCK7 acts on RAC1 to drive actin polymerisation at the leading edge. Sustained signalling through this axis is a feature of MET-amplified tumours.

Hepatocyte growth factor binding to the MET receptor tyrosine kinase drives the proliferation, survival, scattering and morphogenesis of epithelial cells, and much of that output runs through RAS. This branch describes how activated MET converts receptor phosphorylation into GTP loading on HRAS, KRAS and NRAS, and thence into sustained ERK activity that reprogrammes gene expression for motility and growth. The receptor does not contact RAS directly: phosphotyrosines on MET recruit the adaptors GRB2 and SHC1, or scaffolds such as RANBP9, which in turn bring in the guanine nucleotide exchange factor SOS1 to catalyse GDP-to-GTP exchange. Signalling continues from endosomes after receptor internalisation, and binding of MUC20 or RANBP10 to MET dampens the response. Constitutive activity of this axis, through MET amplification or mutation, sustains invasive growth in carcinoma and is a target of kinase inhibitor therapy.

ERBB2 (HER2) is a receptor tyrosine kinase whose amplification drives an aggressive subset of breast and gastric cancers, and blocking it is one of the clearest successes of targeted cancer therapy. Two drug classes converge on this receptor: small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as lapatinib, neratinib and afatinib, which occupy the ATP-binding site and shut down catalytic activity, and monoclonal antibodies such as trastuzumab and pertuzumab, which bind the extracellular domain to prevent dimerisation and promote receptor downregulation. Loss of signalling removes the proliferative and survival input normally relayed to PI3K/AKT and MAPK cascades. The accompanying chaperone machinery, HSP90 with its kinase-specific co-chaperone CDC37, stabilises ERBB2 and is itself a drug target, while ERBIN binds the receptor and restrains its signalling. Resistance commonly arises through kinase-domain mutation or bypass activation of related receptors.

MET is a receptor tyrosine kinase activated by hepatocyte growth factor to drive cell scattering, motility, invasive growth and survival, and it becomes oncogenic when amplified or mutated so that it signals excessively or without ligand. Because MET activation also emerges as an escape route in tumours treated against related receptors such as EGFR, blocking it matters both as a primary therapy and as a way to overcome acquired resistance. Pharmacological inhibition of MET activation covers the two ways this axis is drugged: monoclonal antibodies that intercept HGF or occupy the receptor ectodomain and prevent ligand-induced dimerisation, and small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitors that block catalytic activity and downstream phosphorylation. The outcome is loss of MET autophosphorylation and of the adaptor recruitment that would otherwise feed proliferative and invasive signalling in solid tumours carrying MET-driven lesions.

Neuregulins and EGF-family ligands such as betacellulin, epiregulin and HB-EGF activate the receptor tyrosine kinase ERBB4, and one of the main routes out of the activated receptor is the adaptor SHC1, which converts receptor phosphorylation into RAS–MAP kinase signalling. This arm supports proliferation, survival and differentiation responses in neural, cardiac and mammary tissue, where neuregulin–ERBB4 signalling shapes synapse formation, heart development and lactational differentiation; disturbance of the axis is linked to schizophrenia susceptibility and to breast cancer. Mechanistically, ligand binding drives receptor dimerisation and autophosphorylation of C-terminal tyrosines that dock SHC1 through its phosphotyrosine-binding domain. ERBB4 then phosphorylates SHC1, creating a site for GRB2, which brings the exchange factor SOS1 to the membrane so that HRAS, KRAS or NRAS are loaded with GTP and the RAF–MEK–ERK cascade is engaged.

After insulin binds its receptor and the complex is internalised, the cell must decide the fate of both partners, and insulin receptor recycling is the route that destroys the hormone while returning the receptor to the cell surface. This sets how long a cell stays insulin-responsive and how quickly circulating insulin is cleared, so it bears directly on insulin sensitivity and on the resistance seen in type 2 diabetes. The vacuolar ATPase, represented here by the full complement of V0 and V1 subunits, pumps protons into the endosome; the resulting acidic pH releases insulin from the receptor, and the freed hormone is degraded by insulin-degrading enzyme and cathepsin D. Phosphatases such as PTP1B and PTPRF strip phosphates from the receptor's activated kinase domain, terminating downstream signalling and restoring a ligand-free receptor to the plasma membrane for another round of stimulation.

When ERBB2 heterodimerizes with EGFR or ERBB4 after growth factor binding, phosphotyrosines in the receptor C-terminal tails become docking sites for the adaptor GRB2, and this is the step that converts ligand binding into RAS-dependent proliferation. GRB2 arrives bound to SOS1, a guanine nucleotide exchange factor that loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS, which in turn switches on RAF and the downstream MAP kinase cascade controlling cell cycle entry, growth and survival. The ligands feeding into this route are the EGF-family and neuregulin growth factors, so the same adaptor step serves epithelial proliferation, cardiac and neural development, and wound repair. Because ERBB2 amplification in breast and gastric cancers raises the number of signalling-competent dimers, GRB2 recruitment is a principal route by which these tumours sustain constitutive MAP kinase output, and it underlies resistance when RAS is mutated downstream.

Ligand-bound EGFR has to convert a phosphotyrosine signal into RAS activation, and the adaptor SHC1 provides one of the two routes by which it does so. SHC1 docks on phosphorylated receptor tails through its SH2 and PTB domains, becomes tyrosine phosphorylated itself, and then recruits GRB2 together with the guanine nucleotide exchange factor SOS1; SOS1 loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS, launching the MAPK cascade that drives proliferation, survival and epithelial migration. The pathway can be triggered by any of the receptor's ligands, including EGF, TGFA, amphiregulin, epiregulin, betacellulin and HB-EGF, several of which are shed from the membrane by proteolysis. Because this is the principal mitogenic output of EGFR, activating mutations in the receptor or in RAS lock it on and are among the commonest drivers of lung, colorectal and head and neck cancers.

PTK6 (BRK) is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase that becomes active downstream of ERBB2, linking growth factor receptor engagement at the plasma membrane to proliferation, migration and survival signalling in epithelial cells. The relationship matters in breast cancer, where ERBB2 amplification and elevated PTK6 co-occur and PTK6 reinforces mitogenic output and resistance to ERBB2-directed therapy. Ligands of the EGF family — EGF, betacellulin, epiregulin and heparin-binding EGF acting on EGFR, and the neuregulins acting on ERBB3 and ERBB4 — drive receptor dimerisation, and ERBB2 serves as the preferred heterodimer partner that couples these complexes to PTK6 activation. Because EGFR and MET also heterodimerise with ERBB2, signals apparently arising from those receptors may be relayed through ERBB2 rather than reaching PTK6 directly. Activated PTK6 then phosphorylates substrates governing cytoskeletal dynamics, STAT-dependent transcription and anti-apoptotic signalling.

GRB7 recruitment is one branch of growth factor signalling through the ERBB2 receptor, engaged when neuregulin binds ERBB3 and drives formation of a ligand-activated ERBB2-ERBB3 heterodimer. Phosphotyrosines in the ERBB3 C-terminal tail create the docking site for the adaptor GRB7, which carries no catalytic activity of its own but links the receptor complex to proliferative and migratory outputs. Through recruitment of SHC1 it contributes to RAS activation and cell growth, and when GRB7 is itself phosphorylated by integrin-activated focal adhesion kinase it feeds into VAV2-dependent RAC1 activation and cytoskeletal remodelling that supports cell motility. The downstream mechanisms remain incompletely defined. This arm matters clinically because GRB7 lies adjacent to ERBB2 on chromosome 17 and is co-amplified with it in breast cancer, coupling receptor overexpression to invasive behaviour as well as to proliferation.

Growth factor signalling through ERBB2 converges on the adaptor SHC1 to switch on RAS and the RAF/MAP kinase cascade, driving proliferation and survival in epithelial, cardiac and neural tissues; amplified ERBB2 in breast and gastric cancer makes this route a major oncogenic output and a drug target. ERBB2 has no ligand of its own and acts as the preferred partner for EGFR, ERBB3 and ERBB4, which bind EGF-family and neuregulin ligands such as betacellulin, epiregulin, HB-EGF and NRG1-4. Dimerisation and trans-autophosphorylation create phosphotyrosine docking sites on the receptor C-tails; SHC1 binds, is itself phosphorylated, and recruits GRB2 with the exchange factor SOS1, which loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS. Protein kinase C isoforms and the phosphatase PTPN12 modulate receptor output, tuning signal strength and duration.

When VEGF acts on VEGFR2, one of the immediate consequences is that blood vessels dilate and leak, and this arm of VEGFR2 signalling explains how that happens. Loosening of endothelial junctions allows plasma protein extravasation and provides the matrix and space into which new vessels sprout, so it is an early step in angiogenesis as well as the basis of oedema in tumours, diabetic retinopathy and inflammation. Two outputs converge here. AKT, activated with PDPK1 and the mTORC2 components RICTOR and MLST8, phosphorylates endothelial nitric oxide synthase, which with calmodulin, HSP90 and caveolin-1 releases nitric oxide to relax smooth muscle. In parallel, VAV proteins activate RAC1 and the PAK kinases to trigger endocytosis of VE-cadherin, dismantling the adherens junction with its catenin and plakoglobin partners and opening the paracellular barrier.

Insulin signalling must be switched off as well as on, and signal attenuation is the step that returns a stimulated cell to baseline after an insulin pulse. Once ligand and receptor dissociate inside the endosome and insulin is degraded in the endosomal lumen, endosome-associated protein tyrosine phosphatases strip phosphate from the activated insulin receptor and from its docking substrates. Dephosphorylation of IRS1 and IRS2 releases the adaptors and exchange factors they recruit — GRB2, SHC1 and SOS1 — so the complexes that feed the ERK arm through MAPK1 and MAPK3 fall apart, and the adaptor GRB10 contributes further negative regulation of the receptor. Loss of this shutdown leaves growth and metabolic signalling running without a hormonal cue, while excessive attenuation blunts insulin action and contributes to insulin resistance, making it part of how glucose homeostasis is kept responsive.

Growth factor receptors of the ERBB family route part of their output into the PI3K-AKT axis, and this branch of ERBB2 signalling is how heterodimers containing ERBB2 promote cell survival, growth and metabolic activity. It matters clinically because ERBB2 amplification in breast and gastric cancer, together with activating PIK3CA mutations, makes tumour cells dependent on this arm for survival and shapes response to HER2-directed therapy. Neuregulins bind ERBB3 or ERBB4 and EGF-family ligands such as betacellulin, epiregulin and HB-EGF bind EGFR, driving heterodimerisation with ERBB2 and tyrosine phosphorylation of the receptor tails. The p85 regulatory subunit docks directly on phosphorylated ERBB3 or ERBB4 CYT1 tails, or indirectly via GRB2 and GAB1 when the partner is EGFR, recruiting the p110 catalytic subunit to generate PIP3 and activate AKT at the membrane.

Growth factor stimulation of the EGF receptor must be converted into a lipid signal if a cell is to activate the AKT survival and growth arm, and assembly of the GAB1 signalosome is how that conversion happens. Any of several ligands — EGF, TGFA, amphiregulin, epiregulin, epigen, betacellulin or HB-EGF — activates EGFR, which binds GRB2; GRB2 in turn brings in the scaffold GAB1, and GAB1 recruits the PI3K regulatory subunit PIK3R1 together with the catalytic subunit PIK3CA. The assembled complex phosphorylates PIP2 to PIP3 at the membrane, triggering AKT-dependent proliferation and resistance to apoptosis. GAB1 also docks the phosphatase PTPN11 and links to SRC-family kinase activity, itself restrained by CSK and the adaptor PAG1, while paxillin ties the complex to adhesion signalling. Excessive flux through this node is a recurring feature of EGFR-driven cancers.

Hepatocyte growth factor binding to the MET receptor tyrosine kinase drives epithelial cell scattering, motility, wound repair and morphogenesis, and the same axis is hijacked in carcinomas where MET is amplified or mutated. One branch of that output runs through the tyrosine phosphatase PTPN11 (SHP2). Activated, autophosphorylated MET recruits GRB2, which brings in the multisubstrate adaptor GAB1; GAB1 in turn docks PTPN11 at the receptor complex, where it becomes tyrosine phosphorylated after HGF stimulation. PTPN11 recruited in this way sustains ERK1/2 activation downstream of MET and supports recruitment and activation of sphingosine kinase, linking receptor engagement to lipid second messenger production and cell scattering. The phosphatase also acts back on MET itself, dephosphorylating receptor tyrosines, so this arm both propagates and limits growth factor signalling toward proliferation and migration.

Insulin's message gets past the receptor only through a docking protein, and IRS activation is that step: the activated insulin receptor recruits IRS1 or IRS2 and phosphorylates them on multiple tyrosines, converting them into membrane-associated scaffolds that assemble downstream effectors. This is what couples insulin binding to PI3K-dependent glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis, and to the Ras-MAP kinase arm controlling growth and gene expression. IRS1 engages the receptor's juxtamembrane phosphotyrosine through its PTB domain, with its PH domain anchoring it to membrane phospholipids, then releases once phosphorylated so that SH2-containing partners can bind. GRB10 competes at the receptor and dampens the output, one of several brakes on the pathway. Loss or serine-phosphorylation-driven inactivation of IRS proteins underlies insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, making this node the main site where metabolic signalling is tuned.
